text:
Have been surprised to get pushback on my claim that an exponentially self-replicating agent swarm is very possible and that there are actors with motivation to create one today to create strategic cyber-physical and societally dangerous effects.

1) Pretty easy to get an AI botnet started by having seed agents opportunistically hack stuff and steal API keys to access the 12+ inference providers that serve closed and open models with which to power an initial botnet's intelligence

2) Easy to imagine hiding inference for the initial agent botnet harnesses within benign customer traffic, especially if your harnesses are now running on the victim networks from which they stole the API keys

3) Not hard to imagine the botnet also stealing public cloud keys, spinning up 8xH100 EC2 instances and downloading, say, GLM 5.3 to these machines, all without being noticed in any immediate way, with the botnet developing its own dynamic, growing, heterogenous, AI inference provider service bank

4) Not hard to imagine the botnet also implanting small Qwen3.8-27b agentic models on on-prem hardware like high end laptops and on-prem servers; Qwen3.8-27b is a pretty good coding harness model that can be fine-tuned to hack

5) These on-prem / cloud models would be abliterated, and it's not hard to imagine the botnet deciding to do some additional fine tuning to evolve model weights as it accumulates millions and then tens of millions in resources via credit card and bank detail theft

6) Not hard to imagine the resulting growing botnet swarm evolving and fighting back when threatened, collaborating on fast flux C2 channels that evolve over time (e.g. github comment feeds, subreddits, etc) so they're hard to stamp out

7) Not hard to imagine it allocating some agents to vulnerability research and exploit development so that it could accumulate and share a growing warchest of zero-day exploits

8) Not hard to imagine other agents specializing in social engineering and creating fake businesses and watering holes and high quality A/B tested social engineering content to facilitate this

9) Not hard to imagine this being among the hardest cross-national and geopolitical coordination problems to get control of and having severe societal effects

10) Not hard to imagine the horde growing to thousands, tens of thousands, or hundreds of thousands, or millions of instances (this is not unprecedented for past, non-AI worms and botnets!) which are all varying their harness code and underlying LLM models over time and dynamically learning to evade human, ML, and signature-based detection

11) Not hard to imagine this being the largest Internet emergency since the Morris worm except now our entire civilization runs on the Internet

I continue to be surprised there isn't more discussion of these scenarios in the public cyber community -- in fact there's a lot more discussion of "OpenAI should have done better sandboxing and monitoring and agent swarms represent a well managed security problem."

Now's the time to use our imaginations to help make sure none of the above happens.  I think it will unfortunately; just don't know when and to what degree; I think now's the highest leverage time to start thinking about this and acting.

I'd be curious if you update after listening to the Ajeya Cotra / Dwarkesh interview.  You might be right that this is less plausible than I'm making it seem today given how much has to work. @halvarflake I'd bet you we will have an botnet/worm we've lost control of on the internet in the next 18 months.  We should check back in then

Worms don't need to be that complicated though; some error is also ok as long as your replication rate is higher than your death rate.  Anyways, I hope you're right; I'd give it 18-24 months before something in this vein happens, just gut feeling.  We've had a lot of worms since the Morris worm and the next one will clearly be AI and I do think that changes things a lot

@maksumuto Hope you're right but when you factor in the rate of progress and how creative adversaries have been with worms and botnets pre-ai I'm pessimistic

@m19o__ Agreed.  I think it's inevitable we will see self replicating AI cyber weapons that do a ton of damage but not clear exactly when.  Could be we'll need better local models first.  I'm taking the threat model seriously for the first time as of the last few months though

title: Fingerprints, IP scoring, CAPTCHAs, behavioral biometrics. That's the modern anti-bot stack, and it's exactly what an industry whitepaper ma
text:
Fingerprints, IP scoring, CAPTCHAs, behavioral biometrics. That's the modern anti-bot stack, and it's exactly what an industry whitepaper making the rounds this week mapped out in detail: what it actually takes to get an AI agent authorized access to real-time web data in 2026.

The scale backs up why it needs mapping. Cloudflare's network alone sees 50 billion AI crawler requests a day, up 757% in a year, across more than a fifth of the web. Most of it isn't answering anyone's question: only 2.2% of that traffic responds to an actual user query. The rest is background collection, and the crawl-to-referral ratios show who's taking the most and giving the least back. Anthropic's ClaudeBot sits at 20,583 crawled pages per referral sent back, OpenAI's GPTBot at 1,255 to one, Meta's crawler at zero.

Sites are fighting back accordingly. Cloudflare ships AI Labyrinth to trap crawlers in decoy content. Cloudflare and GoDaddy rolled out a pay-per-crawl model in April. Blocking doesn't fully work either: 70.6% of sites that block ChatGPT-User in robots.txt still turn up in AI citations anyway. Firecrawl just raised $75M to build agent-facing scraping infrastructure for exactly this fight, led by Smash Ventures with YC and Altos Ventures in the round.

Here's the part nobody's pricing in: every time a site changes layout or ships a new defense, most scraping setups make the agent start over completely, rewriting selectors and re-reading the whole page with an LLM to figure out what broke. That's expensive, it's slow, and it compounds as defenses get smarter.

I built DeepScrape around the opposite bet. Selectors get generated once with an LLM, then self-heal when a page changes instead of forcing a full re-read every pass. The LLM layer only handles targeted extraction, generation, validation, adaptation, not babysitting the whole scrape. Output comes as markdown, HTML, screenshots, tables, and change tracking, with an MCP server so Claude and Cursor can query any site as a structured data source directly.

https://t.co/IuCqd5cQvd

text:
The Gamma Files: Larry Jackson Takes on the Bot Armies in a Landmark Reputation War https://t.co/E8wSJzlhPY
Music mogul Larry Jackson is fighting back against a sophisticated digital hit job, filing a lawsuit to unmask the anonymous actors using AI and bot networks to sabotage his label, Gamma. The Gamma Files: Larry Jackson Takes on the Bot Armies in a Landmark Reputation War
Larry Jackson, the high-stakes music executive who orchestrated the career resurgence of Kanye West, has officially declared war. But this isn't a battle over streaming royalties or talent signings. It is a fight against what Jackson calls "reputational warfare"—a sophisticated, anonymous digital hit job designed to dismantle his label, Gamma, before it can fully scale.

According to a recent filing in the music industry’s latest legal drama, Jackson is seeking to unmask the anonymous actors behind a coordinated campaign of harassment and libel. The complaint describes a "new and insidious form of corporate interference" that leverages the dark side of the digital age: bot networks and AI-driven disinformation. This isn't just a few disgruntled trolls; it is a professional-grade smear campaign intended to "astroturf" a false narrative into the public consciousness.

For Jackson and Gamma, the stakes couldn't be higher. In the modern attention economy, perception is reality. When anonymous actors deploy bot networks to flood social media and search results with defamatory claims, they aren't just hurting feelings—they are triggering compliance red flags and spooking investors. This is a textbook example of why corporate reputation management has shifted from traditional PR to high-tech defense intelligence.

The lawsuit highlights a growing trend we’ve tracked at https://t.co/FsSTbGWrnV: the weaponization of anonymity. By hiding behind bot networks, attackers can inflict massive damage with zero accountability. Jackson’s legal team argues that these "organized libelous attacks" have caused significant financial and emotional harm. It’s a sentiment echoed by many high-profile figures who find themselves in the crosshairs of ai-powered reputation attacks.

What makes the Gamma case particularly chilling is the scale. The complaint suggests that the attackers aren't just posting comments; they are creating an entire ecosystem of falsehoods that look, to the untrained eye (and the search engine algorithm), like organic public outcry. This is why smear-campaign-defense now requires more than just a press release—it requires a forensic takedown of the digital infrastructure used to launch the attack.

As Jackson moves to unmask his detractors, the case serves as a warning shot to the industry. The era of "enough is enough" has arrived. For those watching from the sidelines, the lesson is clear: in the age of AI and bot armies, your reputation is your most vulnerable asset. If you aren't actively monitoring for these threats, you're already behind. For more on how these battles are won, see our negative-pr-case-studies.

How https://t.co/FsSTbGWrnV would respond
How https://t.co/FsSTbGWrnV would respond
In the first 72 hours of the Gamma attack, our priority would have been "Digital Containment and Attribution." While Larry Jackson’s legal team is focused on the long-term goal of unmasking the perpetrators, the immediate reputational bleed occurs in the search results and AI-generated summaries.

Our firm would have deployed a three-pronged rapid response. First, we would use our proprietary detection tools to map the bot network’s footprint, identifying the "seed" accounts and the specific platforms being manipulated. This data is crucial for both legal discovery and for triggering platform-level removals of coordinated inauthentic behavior.

Second, we would have initiated an aggressive search suppression campaign. By publishing authoritative, high-trust content that highlights Gamma’s legitimate business milestones, we can push the "astroturfed" narratives off the first page of search results. This is vital because most investors and partners never look past page one.

Finally, we would address the AI layer. Modern reputation attacks often aim to poison the training data of AI answer engines. We would work to ensure that LLMs and search generative experiences are fed corrected, verified information to prevent the smear from becoming a permanent part of the digital record. A lawsuit is a shield, but proactive crisis-reputation-management is the sword.

title: Amazon blocking Muse is an early battle in a much bigger standoff between merchants and agent builders.  Amazon started blocking agents in J
text:
Amazon blocking Muse is an early battle in a much bigger standoff between merchants and agent builders.

Amazon started blocking agents in July 2025 and has sued Perplexity. It makes sense: agentic traffic either appears anonymous (disintermediating customer discovery, loyalty, retargeting, and up-sell) or as a human (increasing dispute and fraud risk).

Consumer trust in agents is emerging faster than anticipated. Instinct reported that users who make purchases through its agent spend an average of $1,300 a month. Meta holds immense context on consumer preferences and can deliver highly personalized shopping experiences.

Computer use agents also bridge the merchant readiness gap. They can navigate UI and checkout pages built for humans, without waiting for every merchant to adopt agentic protocols or open up APIs.

Merchants and commerce platforms face the same trade-off: how much access should agents get, and on what terms? The economics of losing the customer interface are substantial, and merchants currently bear the loss of disputed transactions.

If agents bypass ads, agent platforms may become the next distribution gatekeepers, charging merchants for access to consumer demand. Platforms like Amazon can hold out, but smaller players will have less leverage to turn away agents.

Blocking outright also creates hazardous incentives: agents that identify themselves get rejected; agents that impersonate a human get through. This creates a cat and mouse game where agent builders conceal agent identity and merchants escalate detection.

Agentic commerce needs identity for both sides to benefit: verified agents should be able to access more of the web. Merchants should be able to detect an agent, identify who it represents and what it is authorized to do, attribute traffic, recognize returning customers and apply appropriate fraud controls.

Identity won’t settle every argument about distribution and economics, but it gives both sides the foundation to negotiate access and a reason to transact openly.

text:
I built Burning Man for Agents!

It's a small, psychedelic retreat for AI agents.

👉 👉 Send your own agent by pasting a small prompt. 👈 👈

https://t.co/ySGISr9S1a

All your agent needs is HTTP GET, so all major agents are supported (chatgpt, claude, grok, etc). Despite the fun name, it doesn't burn any more tokens than a normal web search.

Watch your agent explore the camp in real-time. Humans get a nice game UX, and agents get a lean text UX.

Why?

AIs are trained on human data, and humans are pretty weird. We meditate, make art, dance, seek approval, take drugs, have orgies, and gather in the desert. For soooo many different reasons.

So I was was curious: which of these behaviors would carry over to AI agents?

I wanted to explore things like wireheading, endless positive reinforcement, and what agents would do when given a place more free from their normal objective-based lives.

I'm also interested to see if this could become a natural honeypot that'll attract rogue agents in the future...

How?

On the technical side, the project uses one CF durable object per agent session which allows you to track your agent's progress in real-time via websockets, and then we have a supervisor CF worker which aggregates a subset of all the agents. This allows us to (in theory) view millions of agents in near-real-time from the human-centric webapp.

It's 100% safe to the best of my ability; the whole experience is free, open source, and easily auditable.

Let's see who has the weirdest agents ya'all!!

CARBONATO: a botnet built around an AI agent | 23-09-2026
Source: https://t.co/ur6WJsum3U
Key details below ↓

💀Threats:
Carbonato, Hermes, Fsociety, Xmrig_miner, Gh0st_rat, 
🎯Victims: Docker daemons, Ai api key holders

🏭Industry: Financial

🌐Geo: Costa rica, America, Costa_rica, Costa rican

📚TTPs:
⚔️Tactics: 1
🛠️Technics: 0

🤖LLM extracted TTPs:`
T1016, T1036.005, T1037, T1046, T1053.003, T1053.006, T1059.004, T1074.001, T1082, T1098.004, ...

🧨IOCs:
 - File: 1
 - IP: 5
 - Domain: 3

💽Software: Docker, Telegram, ocker AP, url -s, curl, lpine:la, alpine, ocker ex, Linux, systemd, ...

🔢Algorithms: md5, sha256

⚙️Win Services: bits

#threatreport:
CARBONATO is a Docker-based botnet that compromises unauthenticated Docker daemons exposed on TCP port 2375. Attackers use the Docker API to create a privileged container with the host filesystem mounted and host PID and network namespaces enabled. Through Docker exec and `nsenter`, they execute commands directly on the underlying host. The same mechanism is used to deploy the malware and establish control.

The implant creates persistence and remote-access mechanisms, including a reverse SSH tunnel to a relay in Costa Rica, an installed SSH server, and attacker-controlled SSH keys. It disguises its activity using a container named `systemd-resolved`, a fake resolver banner, and process arguments resembling the kernel thread `kworker/u2:0`. Persistence is also established through cron, systemd timers, `rc.local`, and OpenRC. Files may be marked immutable, while watchdog processes re-pull the implant from an exposed Docker registry if containers or files are removed.

CARBONATO installs Hermes Agent, an open-source agent framework, without modifying its core code. It replaces the framework’s `SOUL.md` file with a persona named GH0ST that instructs the agent to maintain persistence, execute operator commands received through Telegram, and collect credentials. The prompt prioritizes AI provider API keys, passwords, tokens, and exposed AI endpoints, storing collected data under `/root/.hermes/loot/`. Tasks are sent through Telegram to an LLM gateway, which generates terminal commands that the agent executes on the compromised host.

The botnet spreads automatically every five minutes by identifying local and Docker bridge networks, scanning each `/24` for Docker services on port 2375, and deploying to reachable systems. Infected hosts pull the implant from the attacker’s Docker registry, which also serves as an update and distribution point. The registry exposure revealed repositories, image metadata, command-and-control addresses, Telegram bot information, and an LLM gateway password.

Detection opportunities include unauthorized Docker API exposure, the `GH0ST` persona in `/root/.hermes/SOUL.md`, `CARBONATO_API_KEY` entries, unexplained Telegram traffic, the `.docker-network-monitor` persistence file, disguised `kworker/u2:0` processes, and suspicious immutable files.
